source: Add the x-parts and the y-parts, then find the size and direction of the result.
Students add magnitudes directly, so 3 N and 4 N at right angles give 7 N instead of 5 N.

Two pushes on a box, two legs of a trip, a boat's velocity plus a river's current: vectors keep needing to be added. Arrows can't simply be added like numbers, because directions matter. Splitting each into components turns the problem back into ordinary arithmetic.

To add vectors, add their $x$-components and add their $y$-components: $R_x = A_x + B_x$, $R_y = A_y + B_y$. Then $R = \sqrt{R_x^2 + R_y^2}$, and its direction comes from $\tan^{-1}(R_y/R_x)$, checked against the quadrant.

Placing the arrows head to tail, the total east-west movement is the sum of each arrow's east-west part, and likewise north-south; the directions along one axis don't interfere with the other. Rebuilding the resultant from its two perpendicular parts is a right triangle again, so the Pythagorean theorem gives its size and inverse tangent gives its angle.
3 N plus 4 N at right angles: the resultant is 5 N at 53.1°, not 7 N.
A drone flies $9\ \text{m}$ east, then $12\ \text{m}$ north. Find the size and direction of its displacement.
A resultant has $R_x = -6$ and $R_y = 8$. What is its direction from $+x$?
A calculator gives $\tan^{-1}(8/-6) \approx -53.1^\circ$, which points into quadrant IV.
But $R_x < 0$ and $R_y > 0$ puts the vector in quadrant II. Add $180^\circ$: $126.9^\circ$.

Adding magnitudes directly, so $3\ \text{N}$ and $4\ \text{N}$ at right angles "make $7\ \text{N}$". That is only true when the vectors point the same way. Check: the resultant is never larger than the sum of the sizes and never smaller than their difference, and it equals the sum only when they are lined up.
